A proof is given on page 25. This theorem enables one to easily compute matrix repre-
sentations of principal elements in a reflection system given a reflection diagram. We use
this theorem along with other results to generate a table of mixed-sign An-type Coxeter
graphs (with n < 6) and associated principal elements along with the spectral radii of the
principal elements, see Table B.1 and Table B.2.
We also study structures of mixed-sign Coxeter groups. As mentioned, classical Coxeter
groups have a particulary nice presentation which one can easily read offfrom the associated
Coxeter graph. For general reflection systems and mixed-sign Coxeter systems finding a
group presentation from the bilinear form and generating matrices is not straightforward.
We show that mixed-sign Coxeter groups are like classical Coxeter groups in the sense that
they are generated by involutions and have pairwise relations between the generators.
A result from [BB05] shows that if a mixed-sign Coxeter system satisfies a property called
the Deletion Property (see Property 3.7) then it is a classical Coxeter system. However,
unlike classical Coxeter systems, Lemma 3.21 illustrates that there is a mixed-sign Coxeter
system which does not have the Deletion Property. In Section 3.3 we use this example
to create a family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems which also do not satisfy the Deletion
Property.

Another way in which mixed-sign Coxeter systems differ from classical Coxeter systems is
in the behavior of their principal elements. C. McMullen [McM02] showed that the minimal
spectral radius of a Coxeter element arising from a classical Coxeter group is either 1 or
Lehmer’s number. Lehmer’s number is approximately 1.17628, it is the largest real root of
the polynomial
McMullen showed this by noticing that the spectral radius of a particular class of Coxeter
elements called the bipartite Coxeter elements always minimizes the spectral radius among
all other Coxeter elements in the Coxeter group. Of course, bipartite Coxeter elements
are only well defined when the Coxeter graph is bipartite. McMullen defines the bipartite
eigenvalue of a Coxeter system; this algebraic number is the spectral radius of a bipartite
Coxeter element, for a bipartite Coxeter graph. McMullen generalizes this notion to any
Coxeter system, he defines the bipartite eigenvalue using the spectral radius of the bilinear
form of the Coxeter system. McMullen proves the bipartite eigenvalue of a Coxeter system
is less than the spectral radius of every Coxeter element in the Coxeter group. The story is
much different for mixed-sign Coxeter systems.

groups. The converse is not true, in general. The reflection diagram gives us more infor-

Lehmer’s problem asks the question if there exists a c > 1 such that every polynomial
f with integer coefficients and M(f) > 1 has M(f) ≥c. Currently, no polynomial has
been found with a smaller Mahler measure than Lehmer’s number. The problem has been
reduced to studying the Mahler measure of reciprocal polynomials, see [Smy] and [Hir09].
Since every principal polynomial is reciprocal, principal polynomials make good candidates
to further study the problem. Lehmer’s number makes an appearance in Coxeter groups as
it is the minimal spectral radius of a Coxeter element in (W, S, B(E10)). One motivation
for studying the topics in this paper is to emulate and generalize these results along with
other notions from classical Coxeter theory.

The Deletion or Exchange Properties are interchangeable characteristics which define
classical Coxeter systems in the following sense.
Let (W, S, B) be a reflection system. Suppose that W is a group generated

2. (W, S, B) satisfies the Deletion Property.

• If w has eigenvalues which are greater than 1 then the Coxeter system is hyperbolic
or higher-rank.
